questions.prompt: Which elementary sort runs in O(n) on already-sorted (or nearly-sorted) input?

options.text: None — they are all always Θ(n²)
Selection sort, but only for reverse-sorted input

questions.explanation: Insertion sort (and early-exit bubble sort) does almost no shifting on sorted data, giving O(n) best case. Selection sort has no best-case speedup.

questions.prompt: Which of the three elementary sorts is NOT stable in its standard form?
questions.explanation: The standard swap-based selection sort can reorder equal keys, so it is not stable. Insertion and bubble sort are stable.

questions.prompt: Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Insertion sort's best case is O(n)
All three elementary sorts are in-place (O(1) extra space)
Selection sort performs only O(n) swaps
Bubble sort's worst case is O(n log n)

questions.explanation: Insertion is O(n) best case, all three are in-place, and selection makes only O(n) swaps. Bubble sort's worst case is Θ(n²), not O(n log n).

questions.prompt: A sort is called ______ if equal elements keep their original relative order. (one word)
questions.explanation: Stability preserves the prior ordering of equal keys — important when sorting records by successive fields.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of inserting one element (the key) during insertion sort.

items.text: Take the next element as the key
Shift larger sorted elements one place right
Place the key in the resulting gap

questions.explanation: Each outer step takes the next key, slides larger elements right to open a gap, and drops the key into place — keeping the prefix sorted.

questions.prompt: Match each sort with a distinguishing property.
questions.explanation: Each sort has a signature: insertion is adaptive, selection minimizes swaps, bubble swaps neighbors, and Timsort is the O(n log n) production default.
